title: Does Stopping Your SIP During a Market Crash Actually Help?
meta_title: Does Stopping Your SIP During a Market Crash Actually Help? | Aperture
summary: Stopping your SIP when markets fall costs you cheap units rupee cost averaging was built to buy. Here's when pausing actually makes sense in India.

content:
Stopping your SIP when markets fall doesn't protect your money. It costs you the very thing a SIP is designed to deliver: cheap units. The months when fear spikes and investors stop are, mathematically, the months a SIP does its most useful work. Pausing locks in fewer units and breaks the compounding chain, often for good.

Key Takeaways

  • India's SIP stoppage ratio crossed 100% in March and April 2026, more SIPs closed than opened.
  • Stopping forfeits rupee cost averaging at exactly the moment it delivers the most value.
  • Most investors who pause wait for prices to recover, then buy back in at higher NAVs.
  • Stop only if income drops, a goal is met, or the fund has a structural problem. Not because markets fell.
  • SIP inflows hit a record Rs 32,297 crore in August 2026, showing most long-term investors stayed put.

Does stopping your SIP during a market crash actually help?

No, it doesn't. For almost every investor, stopping a SIP during a correction does the opposite of protecting wealth. A SIP works by buying a fixed rupee amount every month: when NAV drops, that amount buys more units. When the market recovers, those extra units multiply. Pausing forfeits the cheapest buying window, which is the whole point of the method.

The larger risk isn't even the missed months. It's what happens after. People who stop almost always wait for markets to "stabilize" before restarting. By then, NAV has recovered, and they buy fewer units for the same money. The fear-stop-wait-rejoin loop is one of the most expensive moves a retail investor makes.

What actually happens when you pause a SIP?

Say you run a Rs 5,000 monthly SIP in a large-cap equity fund. The market drops 18% over five months. If you pause, you skip five months of buying at below-average NAV. If you continue, each Rs 5,000 buys roughly 20 to 22% more units than it did before the fall.

Over a 20-year horizon at a 12% CAGR, missing six monthly instalments early in the investment period can reduce the final corpus by an estimated Rs 1.5 to 2.8 lakh, depending on when the pause falls. Earlier pauses hurt more because compounding has longer to multiply the missing units.

Investors who stop definately intend to restart. But they wait for things to settle, and by then, NAV is usually already recovering. Most of the cheap units are gone. So they rejoin at higher prices, buy fewer units per instalment, and miss most of the upswing. The delay can cost two or three years of compounding at the cheapest possible prices.

Stopping SIP vs. Continuing SIP: A direct comparison

FactorStopping your SIPContinuing your SIP
Units bought during crashZeroAbove average (lower NAV)
Re-entry timingUsually at recovered pricesNot applicable
Long-term corpus impactMeaningfully lowerOn track
Behavioral riskHigh (the wait-then-rejoin trap)Low (automatic, no decision needed)
Right choice whenIncome drops or goal is metMarket falls and fear spikes

Why do so many Indian investors stop at the worst time?

Because loss feels real even when it's notional. When your portfolio balance falls 15%, the pain is immediate and visible. The SIP outflow, by contrast, feels optional. So stopping feels protective, not harmful.

AMFI data shows the SIP stoppage ratio crossed 100% in March and April 2026 as Indian markets corrected. By August 2026, the ratio had eased back to 81.1%, with monthly SIP contributions reaching a record Rs 32,297 crore. Most investors who stayed in emerged better positioned than those who paused and rejoined later.

The behavioral pull is real. Research in finance consistently shows that a notional loss registers as roughly twice as painful as an equivalent gain feels good. Watching your portfolio turn red by Rs 20,000 feels much worse than watching it grow by Rs 20,000 feels good. That asymmetry pushes people toward stopping, even when stopping is objectively the more costly action.

And then the second trap hits. By the time things feel settled and safe again, the recovery has already occured. The investors who waited to rejoin found prices had moved back up faster than expected. That's not a coincidence. Markets tend to recover sharply before the news cycle catches up.

When stopping your SIP actually makes sense

Three situations justify stopping, in order of how often they genuinely apply:

  • Income drops or cash flow is tight. Job loss, a pay cut, or a medical emergency means the SIP payment may genuinely be unaffordable. Stop without guilt, and restart when income stabilizes. No long-term benefit is worth going into overdraft or skipping essential expenses.
  • The goal this SIP was funding is met. You started it to build a seperate corpus for a house down payment, and you've hit the target. Close it rather than letting money accumulate in a fund with no defined next purpose.
  • The fund has a structural problem. The fund manager left, the mandate has changed, or it has meaningfully underperformed its benchmark and peer group for two or more consecutive years. Check Value Research or MorningStar before deciding, not just recent NAV movement.

Markets going down is not on that list. A falling market is, counterintuitively, a SIP's best working environment.

Note: This post is general information, not personalized financial advice. Consult a SEBI-registered investment advisor for decisions specific to your situation.

Frequently asked questions about stopping a SIP

Is it bad to stop a SIP for just one month?

One skipped instalment has a small direct impact, but it tends to normalize pausing. Most investors who skip one month stop for six or more before restarting. If cash flow allows, continuing is almost always the right call. One month of SIP units bought at lower prices can compound meaningfully over 15 to 20 years.

What if markets keep falling after I continue my SIP?

Then your next instalment buys even more units at even cheaper prices. A prolonged fall is not a warning sign for a SIP investor. It's a longer window to accumulate discounted units before the eventual recovery. Rupee cost averaging works specifically because you don't need to predict the bottom.

Should I increase my SIP when markets fall?

If your emergency fund is intact and you have surplus cash, a small lump sum addition during a correction can improve long-term returns. Stepping up your regular SIP amount by 10% annually, regardless of market conditions, is simpler and nearly as effective over a long horizon.

What is the SIP stoppage ratio in India right now?

As of August 2026, AMFI data shows the ratio at 81.1%, down from over 100% in March and April. A ratio below 100% means new SIP registrations outnumber closures. The drop from above 100% to 81% across five months shows how quickly sentiment shifted as markets steadied.

Does stopping a SIP trigger a tax event?

Stopping future instalments doesn't trigger tax. But if you redeem existing units within one year of purchase, equity fund gains are taxed as short-term capital gains at 20%. Units held longer than one year qualify for the long-term capital gains rate of 12.5% on gains above Rs 1.25 lakh per year.

The short version

Stopping your SIP when markets fall is one of the most common and expensive mistakes Indian investors make. You give up cheap units, break compounding, and nearly always buy back in at higher prices. Stop only when income genuinely drops, a goal is reached, or the fund has a real problem. Otherwise, when the portfolio turns red, the most valuable thing to do is nothing.
